en: Having saluted Gaṇapati, the destroyer of the net of faults, who bestows the awakening of the phonemes of the supreme state through constant practice,
I here extract this nectar of the *Āraṇyaśikṣā* from the ocean of the new *Śikṣā* for the sake of the assembly of Brahmins.
But here, all the various groups are clearly described in their entirety. || 2 ||
Sentences with initial acute accents (ādyudātta) are cited by groups of one, two, three, and so on,
for the purpose of removing the doubts of students;
however, wherever the mention of the beginning, middle, or end is made, [the following applies].
However, the words *yat* and *tat* are always acutely accented on their first syllable.

It should be understood that this refers to "of sentences," because there is a single hearing from the Śruti: "If you know anything beyond this, which is the highest goal of merit" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.15). || 5 ||
If these [beings] are not always superior to this image of a woman,
and if those [others] there are not superior to that which is struck by the fierce neck according to one's merit— then you will not attain the supreme state, nor any other high station.
Now, may we overcome the waters, the Mahānāmnīs, the Marīcīs, and the Adas;
that which is named "Thou" (Yat), and where this [is], what is the one-hearing and the waterless?
In the month of Āṣāḍha, there will be food for one who is angry, and famine in the winter months.
Clad in white, he gladdens the day and the year;
I ask about the two winds from both sides, the expanses, and the dogs of the city.
The red, the skin, and the clouds—O All-Conqueror, may this be auspicious for you.
O divine son, O Nāsatyas, from that fierce and extensive affliction, Indra, having been satisfied by your exhilarating and subtle drops, has emerged victorious. 10.
And in Varuṇasyānavarṇe and ariṣṭaṃ nṛmuṇaṃ ratham,
he observed that the sentences were udātta on the first syllable according to the count of unity.
The Lord laughed at Vārada, who had come to him;
he indeed binds those who revile him with his tongue, as if these worlds were free from fear.
By means of the *kālas* (time-units), this semen—Indra—is not overcome by any being; it is the double (*dvika*).
Now he speaks of the triads (*trikāni*): "The white and black [are] the head, and the Maruts are the head. (13)
The mantras beginning with "tava" belong to all of them; these [mantras] are not deficient in their threefold nature.
Parjanya, Śiśira, the meters, Rodasī, Apeta-vī, Anūha, Sahasrākṣa, Apām-gṛha, Bhūmi, and the four Brāhmaṇas—
these follow the one-year-old [calf] by means of a single [verse], having taken their stand upon the non-existent. 15.
The ninefold group of the most excellent [elements] is atom by atom; likewise, there are six efforts and ten.
The five, the final six of the Viṣūvats, the Smṛti, the seven of the Naktas and Amdas, the one spoken as the beginning of the Sukhādis, the two Tātas, and the eleven—
those in which there are seventeen for him, and eighteen as well. (17)
The seven and twenty Āditya gods—these indeed are they;
and those thirty-three who are said to be "in whom the suns [shine]," according to their own desire, are thirty-three. (18)
From here onwards, there are fifty-two sections (anuvākas) beginning with the Āśātikās;
then the Saṃvatsara, the Ādityas, and five others among these.
O Gārgya, there will be seven suns at the end of the eon, and it will indeed be a marvel when that occurs. || 20 ||
The Bhadra meter is not mounted upon these [feet]; here, indeed, there is no *iyā*.
The *dīrghayu*, *upaṅti*, and *rādhā* meters shine forth clearly;
Agni, with eight ruddy horses, is like a king accompanied by the *pravargya* ceremony.
Speak; the sound of the breath, possessing the strength of movement, destroys the darkness of ignorance.
"You make it second," thus [he says] regarding that which has appeared before him in universal forms;
and the two [stotras], beginning with the Cakṣur-mātra, which belong to me as if to a thief— by this [verse],
he makes one [of them] possess a vimāna, and both [the other] also possess a nidhana.
That which is without hands is its action; that which is without night is the primordial Brahman, the beginningless heaven.
Or rather, this [syllable] is like the head and so forth, a vowel equal to the two [consonants] ending in the letter 'u'.
Or [it is accomplished] by seven, or by two, or by those which are these, or by that which is within me.
In this world, he will not perish;
in the other world, he shall be victorious along with his kin; and here, he shall possess the triad beginning with food.
"akārya-kodhṛtāsi"—these two [words] belong to me, the Sovereign (Īśvarī).
This much [is the rule] regarding the sequence of identical accents, ending with the acute (udātta) following a grave (anudātta).
Now, he states those beginning with the acute (ādyudātta) that are joined with two circumflex (svarita) accents:
O Brahmin, you do not sleep; you gladden the entire city.
Or that which is "not suffering" (aduḥkha), and likewise "white" (śveta) and "without purpose" (anartha) regarding Agni's head;
as well as the pair beginning with "not harsh" (alūkṣa), and the pair beginning with "from day" (ahna). || 28 ||
One should understand that *abhūti* has two meanings and is udātta-accented on its first syllable;
likewise, *tvaṃśete* is not derived from *sarva*, and it indeed gladdens those who are white (*śveta*).
Indeed, those who are around and those who are like oxen—as is your head, so it is;
and as for the two days, likewise twice the noble and once the high in the middle.

Then, O Brahman, you should indeed bestow upon him the city of Brahmā (brahmapura), which has the word "agni" at the beginning, is doubly udātta in the middle, has two svarita vowels, and possesses the syllable "na-bhūti. || 31 ||
From all of that [arises] the three-syllabled [mantra]; from Ucca and others, the single-syllabled and middle [mantras].
Paṭara, Nijaha, Viṣṇu, Kaśyapa, Paśu, and Agni [are the deities]. || 32 ||
The pentad beginning with "ubhayānaśṛtāseha coddhṛta" and the dyad beginning with "śarīre uttama," as well as that which is my mind— 33.
The collection of statements such as "the Goddess," "one whose semen flows upward," "Saramā," "that one," "O Aśvins," "dark," "twice-born," "noble," and "lowly" has been cited. (34)
If one has the capacity, one should provide two Prasendra-dhenu cows according to one's means.
"Śrīr me vidyā prajā paśu" and so forth—these follow after the words with euphonic junction (sandhi);
and there is the application "yaḥ pūrvasya," as well as [the mantras] "śriyā hriyā bhiyā rasaḥ. (36)

Oṃ; from that beginning, after six [syllables] there is the great darkness (mahāndhya), followed by the svarita accent and so forth; one should enter [the path] with the southern power (dakṣiṇā-śakti) and the inhalation (vāna), as well as the barley-grains (yava). || 37 ||

"Let the self-study of the *devagāyatrī*—which begins with a circumflex accent (*svarita*) and ends with two acute accents (*udātta*)—be undertaken, for it is the very essence of the meters and is free from the fear of harshness. (38)
Indeed, the words [ending in] *e* and *o*, which have their own inherent vowels (*svarāṇi*) immediately preceding them destroyed, are as already stated;
here, when a low-pitched *i* (*nīcekāra*) follows an *i* (*ekāra*) belonging to a vowel (*dvijasvara*). (39)

In certain cases, the vowel *ī* is formed through euphonic combination (*sandhi*) as a closely joined (*praśliṣṭa*) circumflex (*svarita*). For example, in *evāhīndratva-bhīddhoktam*, there are two instances of the closely joined circumflex.
In the Āraṇyaka, however, it is said that the acute accent (udātta) occurs at the end of a sentence.
O you of great majesty, you do not fall; you arise before them as the one who pierces through the darkness. || 41 ||
The verses beginning with "anṛṇāścitram yaḥ," "tityā," and "namo brahme" are indeed found in the Svādhyāyabrāhmaṇa; if one does not know them, [the following] is the supreme [substitute]. (42)
In the village and at midday, how many [recitations] should there be for him?
One, two, five, and two [times] the utterance of "namo vāce. (43)
In the *Hemapūrvatantra*, in the *Sahapraśna*, and in the *Pitṛmedha* and *Ambhas* [sections], a *ḍa* situated between vowels with their natural (*prākṛta*) accent undergoes the change to *la*. (44)
In the phrase "vitudasya," there should be the substitution of *datva*; after the word "pretya," there is indeed the substitution of *aikāra*.
Furthermore, "bhadraṃ ca saha saṃjñānam" and "lokastubhyam" follow in sequence. (45)
These five questions shall be known by the designation "Kāṭhaka," and no others;
therefore, when [the word] *pṛkta* follows *śabda*, it is not obtained before [it reaches] *kare*.
In the case of a conjunction with a sibilant (ūṣman), the prohibition [of doubling] is not desired there;
therefore, the letter *r* following the word *tena* does not undergo doubling, nor does the letter following it. (47)

In this context, within the *kāraka* suffixes beginning with *dhiṣṇya*, the forms *rātryām*, *anvāpitrya*, *tathābhartryoḥ*, and *janayitryaḥ* occur; here, neither the vowel *ī* nor *yaṇ* [substitution] takes place.
In the Kāṭhaka texts, an anusvāra is desired after the word *vāsaḥ* when it is followed by *kare*;
likewise, [anusvāra occurs] before *śanau* as in *svaḥ*, and elsewhere before *śañiri* as in *suvaḥ*.

The kampas are indeed determined to be of two kinds: the *svāra* and the *ucca*. Of these two, the *svāra* is considered [to apply] in the *saṃhitā*, while the *ucca* is held [to apply] in the *Āraṇyaka*.
In the three [stomas] beginning with the Aditya, when the Abhinidhata-svara is constant,
the Uccaiḥ-kampa is prescribed as being neither lower nor higher than that.
Likewise, at the end of a word there are tremblings, with the subtle elements (aṇu) struck down at the very end;
for the remainder, there may be either the state of being udātta or its own inherent accent (svarita), according to the established rule.
In the Āraṇyaka, however, there is no *svāra* accent, nor is there the *udātta* in the *saṃhitā*;
in the *Pārakṣudra*, there are no *kampas*, for the *kampa* is of two kinds and not three.
Indraghoṣa and the other seven, Viśīrṣṇī and the other three, and likewise Aṣṭayoni— among these, they know the tone to be the same.
One should recognize the tone as equal wherever there is even a single raised word; for this very recognition of the objects follows those objects exactly as they are.
One should avoid using lotus leaves for the Mahānāmnīs and Indra; likewise, one does not obtain the state of being a knower of the Self by avoiding the moon along with its companions.
When this body, which is subject to much suffering, has been carried away, great indeed are my misfortunes;
yet now my tongue longs for the nectar of immortality as its neighbor. 57.
From the waters [comes] Nāya; I am eternally [the source of] Manuṣya, Brahma-vidyā, and Dā;
Bhīṣā and Kīrti; Nirukta; two by two; and the triad beginning with Śruta in sequence. (58)
In drinking, in the body, in the eyes, in consciousness, and likewise in hearing—the supreme Prāṇa does not attend to these; bliss is fire, and this is the truth.

In these cases, only the two truths are intended; there is no falling into the extremes of high or low, provided that the word "space" (ākāśa) is not used everywhere as a term for the self when it refers to a grammatical euphonic combination (sandhi). 60.
In the same way, if the word "earth" (pṛthivī) does not refer to the head and the tail, it is recited as:
"I shall say that it indicates its own end. (61)
It is said that he recited "dvitīyaḥ," "śaṃ," "astu," and "tvām";
then four beginning with "ahamasmi," and one beginning with "kaścit. (62)
Among these, all those whose final syllables are protracted (pluta) are low;
for there can be no *svāra* or *upaniṣad* accentuation whatsoever in such cases.
It is certain that all [the hymns] end with the question to Nārāyaṇa;
the Viśvā, Agni, and Sāvitra [hymns], as well as the two pairs, are indeed present. 64.
The gods [have taught] one, nine, seven, and sixteen [syllables] as extended (*pluta*) in the *Āraṇyaka*.
Every extended vowel would be high-pitched (*udātta*), except for the final one. (65)

In the inquiry concerning Nārāyaṇa, he generally promises to state the specific details for the sake of clarifying the numerous contradictions regarding the question "in the water" (ambhasi) and so forth;
indeed, the statements beginning with "having a single accent" (eka-śruti) are all explicitly mentioned in full.
He states the definitions of *ekaśruti* and *śrutivākya* in succession:

"Where the accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth are uttered without distinction of the fourfold intonation (*cātuḥsvarya*), and where the sentence is spoken as if it were high-pitched, that is called *ekaśruti*. (67)

In the first word, there is a double accent (dvyucca) or a multiple accent (bahūcca) anywhere; it is heard as having one unraised tone (anudātta), a circumflex (svarita), or a low final and high final (antocca-antacchruti). || 68 ||
If the fourth and fifth syllables are identical to the single final syllable of the preceding word, or to the two final syllables of the preceding sentence, they are designated as *yama*. (69)
If the penultimate syllable is heavy, it is considered "struck" (nihata) therein;
if it is light, it shall be acute (udātta), as is held in the Vedic statements.
The earth, the cow, and Alakṣmī; desire, wrath, and likewise sin;
and Śrī—these six you declared to be the primordial three through the sacrifice and the Veda. (71)
Kāma and Manyu are in the western [face]; both are situated in the middle, excluding the last one.
Likewise, Īśāna also moves within the end, like sesame seeds.
The two [verses] beginning with "stuta" and "gosteyam" are indeed called the "dviśrutāni";
this is the essence of Soma's power, and "namo prācyai" is the "bahuśrutī. (73)
That which is at the beginning of the Veda— the group of two and six, such as the food-sheath (annamaya) and the prāṇa and apāna breaths—
is indeed called "sa-cām" (and that), for it is pronounced with a single accent at the beginning.
In this [verse] ending with "namo vāru," you indeed have all [the syllables];
likewise, these two read themselves as the final portion of the second [chapter]. (75)

To the upward-pointing sprout at the very end, to Agni and the triad beginning with Āditya, to the sesame seeds, to the two knots of the vital breaths, and to the two bases—the thumb and the little finger—salutations, O Hara! (76)
All the Vedic statements are indeed bent toward the [five] fires; the fivefold group ending with Yama is remembered as extending up to the belly of Gāyatrī. (77)
Indeed, from the first yoga up to the fifth, and including the seven final śrutis, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra correspond respectively to these three stages. (78)
"Salutation to Gaṅgā, to the beginning of the lineages, and to those who go to the end of existence;
likewise, these four other scriptural traditions are to be known. (79)
"Entire life" (sarvāyuḥ) is this one [formula], which is recited with a low tone and so forth;
"Oṃ bhūvaḥ," the words beginning with "mouth" (mukha), are indeed five and are all of the highest pitch.
"I am" (ahamasmi) and so forth, as well as three [mantras] excluding the first syllable of "ādi," and those mantras where this occurs, such as "apeta" and likewise "iti. (81)
This self is like a well; obeisance to the other [direction] for the sake of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
All this, beginning with the two udātta accents and so forth, is beyond the Great Splendor (mahas), namely "Om. || 82 ||
Vāsoddhamā, kūjasiddha, maṇimeka, and ṛṣi—these words of this [text] beginning with *udātta* and so forth have been stated as they appear in the Veda. 83.
[He should offer oblations] to Samānasīsa, Dāmni, Avantara,
Tathālaka, Pratnoṣika, and to the two enemies of Savitṛ, as well as to Irapas.
These words beginning with "udagayana" are high and medium;
however, [the following] arise from the lotus-bud, the garland of flames, the horizontal, the upward, and the upward-blowing. (85)
Beyond a hundred and a hundred [of these] everywhere is the supreme *mahasoma*, which is of great splendor;
these grains, with their internal elevations, were described by the Vaidikas.
The word *pramaihā* has two udātta accents; *bhīṣuṇaḥ* has two udātta accents on the middle syllables;
*sahariḥ* would have the udātta on the first syllable; but *śuk* and *śucantau* have the udātta on all syllables.
From each of these [particles], this word has two udātta accents when it occurs at the end of a phrase;
however, when preceded by *upa*, it shall have two udātta accents, as in the examples *iha-iha* and *vavā-hava*.
It is held that at the junction [of words], a word-final udātta vowel becomes low-pitched (nīca);
likewise, in the case of the Pitṛmedha, it occurs in the junctions of the water-rites (ambhas). 89.
Then there was inferiority, and after that, the state of being either one or both;
likewise, there were horses, truth, and the merit-performing Īśāna.
"Whatever is within my mind, and likewise this salutation to the East—these are declared to be single-syllable [mantras] with a nasalized (sandhinīca) junction. (91)
And that which was mentally recited by me, consisting of a thousand verses at most—this indeed has been declared as belonging to Soma, O consumer of the first portion, O Nīlatoyada. 92.

In the two statements "gandhadvārām" and "durātyāśanāśvakrānte," the status of being a *sandhinī* (a cow that has recently calved) should be understood respectively for both phrases in their proper order. 93.
Hunger and thirst [should be offered] in the lotus and so forth, according to the sequence previously mentioned for the three;
likewise, black sesame seeds should be offered on the supreme peak.
Whatever sin one commits during the day, it shall be divided among four [of the preceding days] in successive order;
likewise, whatever [sin] occurs at the beginning of the Veda, it shall be divided among five [of the preceding days] in successive order. (95)

Nārāyaṇa is the great object of knowledge; likewise, there are six [breaths] beginning with *uddhṛta*, and twelve [breaths] consisting of prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, and udāna, in their proper sequence. (96)
Dūrvā grass, śatayoman, Viṣṇu—may that [merit] be in you, O son of Kaśyapa; for by this hand he shall immediately unite me with the imperishable Puruṣa.
O Goddess, one should likewise go to the Viśvaveda ground at the time of twilight;
in this [ground], one should avoid food with the mantra beginning "sahasraśīrṣam."

Among these, one who is most skilled in the knowledge of vowels should recognize that the supreme syllable of the color resulting from the destruction of the junction (sandhi) is itself destroyed, one by one. 99.
"O Kṛṣṇe, protect me who have committed the act of killing a Brahmin;
likewise, 'I am going'—thus Alakṣmī [is dispelled]; the two previously mentioned [evils] are destroyed. (100)
Wherever there is the state of being a pregnant cow, right there is the place of final rest;
having become sinful, O Goddess, they go to the destination of Yama and other such realms. (101)

In the *āraṇya* sections and so forth, as well as at the beginning and end of two [sections], and likewise in three, the wise have prescribed a change of vowel and a change of syllable in the five questions. (102)
The lowliness of the exalted and the exaltation of the base and so forth—indeed, both the Goddess and the Vedas know that to be most abundant on this earth. (103)

The aforementioned [rules] concern the alteration of vowels (*svarānyatva*), whereas the alteration of consonants (*varṇānyatva*) constitutes a transgression (*helana*). Furthermore, the triad beginning with *śikṣā* ought to constitute a single chapter. (104)
The first two [sections] are the Pitṛmedha and Ambhaḥ; these constitute five chapters.
These verses are most auspicious, by the inhalation of which I have been summoned and delivered from my distress. (105)
These gods are indeed long; I myself am immortal.
Five vowels are protracted and long, while four are [so] in the Taittirīyaka. 106.

At the end of those [vowels], that which has a beautiful nose (sunāsikya) is called *raṅga*. In *raṅga* and in a long vowel (*dīrgha*), there is one *mātrā* for each of the *raṅga* and the long vowel respectively.
A *raṅga* and a *pluta* together constitute two *mātrās*, as do a *pluta* and a *raṅga*; according to the opinion of the followers of the Yajurveda, a *raṅgapluta* consists of four *mātrās*. (108)
The anusvāra occurs before the sibilants (ūṣman), the letter *r*, and the vowels;
the nasalized form (*anunāsika*) of the letter *m* occurs before the supreme self (*paramātman*). 109.
In the word "om," that which is the letter *ma* is peace, and likewise, peace is in the supreme;
joined with the two letters *a* and *e*, the letter *e* attains the status of a complete word.
The Praṇava, joined with the three states of peace, attains the status of speech;
having placed it above the *yāyakas*, it is indeed the Sage among sages.
Thus, [the suffix] *asra*, *śīman*, and *kā* are unaccented (*apūrva*), as is the *ṛṣi*;
furthermore, the word *garbha* is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) when followed by *sva*, *svāni*, or another [word], provided it is not at the end of a compound.
The *āditya* and the *anu-vāka*, as well as those consisting of three *anuvākas* beginning with *satya*, end with the word *upaniṣad* preceded by two vowels and followed by the word *dvija*. (113)
For the four groups beginning with the second, there is a ninefold [set] and the initial low-pitched (nīcaka) tone;
in this *anuvāka* beginning with "yo'sau," one should state the remainder as high-pitched (*ucca*) and so forth.
In this Anuvāka, there is no instance of words having an acute accent on the first syllable;
"aham" begins with an anudātta (grave), and "mahān" begins with a svarita (circumflex). 115.

The vowels at the beginning and middle [of a word] are void of attainment through their own names, whereas the seven vowels are eternal by their very nature; the unchanging [consonant] is primordial and indestructible.
The word *akṣara* means "immutable," and it is applied to them even when followed by a higher vowel;
as in the case of the *kṣaipra-svāra* of the letter *i*, [as seen in the mantra] *gāyatrīṃ śrīḥ śriyā hriyā*.
Just as barley, horses, fires, and cattle [are common], where there is the knowledge of the eternal, if there are offspring, those two are the great essence. || 118 ||
In the case of the vowels *e* and *au*, there is a *svāra*; therein, it becomes an *abhinihata*.
When a vowel is accented in *saṃhitā*, if a higher accent follows, it becomes a *prātihata*.
They call this one "ūrdhvaretas" (one whose seed is drawn up), as it is said here: "and *yathā te*.
In that context, the svarita vowel *ū* is joined (*praśliṣṭa*) and is said to signify non-existence (*abhūti*).

In that [Gāyatrī], the *kevala* which is the *svāra* (monotone) and the *pādavṛtta* (metrical by foot) without accumulation, first there is the *tairovyañjanaka* (the accentuation of consonants) in the preceding [syllables]. 121.
In questions concerning the triad beginning with the city, the accentuation should be like that of the *saṃhitā*;
except for sentences such as those in the *ekaśruti* style, everything else should have a uniform accent (*samasvara*).
Indeed, after a vowel ending in 'a', Sadāśiva always attains the form 'oṃ';
likewise, the supreme form of Subrahmaṇya is 'oṃ', and so forth in all cases.
The acute accent (udātta) belongs to the Brahmin caste; the grave (nīca) is said to belong to the Kṣatriya;
the circumflex (svarita) belongs to the Vaiśya caste; and the protracted (pracaya) is declared to be the Śūdra. || 124 ||
The Svaras and the first [classes] are indeed the Brahma-jātis;
the third and the fourth are declared to be the Kṣatra-jātis. || 125 ||
The *uttama* [letters] and likewise the semi-vowels (*antastha*) are proclaimed as belonging to the Vaiśyas;
while the *śūdras* consist of *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, *ca*, the *anusvāra*, and that which is born from the *visarga*. (126)
When their respective classes are uttered, those [classes] are preserved;
if another class were to be spoken, that would be the destroyer of them. (127)
Even if it is pure, knowledge does not shine without its defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa), just as the adornment of ornaments is of no use for a god who lacks life-breath. 128.
Thus has the entire system of vowels and consonants been described for the delight of the learned in the five types of Vedic inquiries;
however, whatever has not been explicitly described here in the Āraṇyaka, all of that should be inferred by the wise for themselves.

In the triad of questions beginning with "cityā," the accent should be like that of the *saṃhitā*; otherwise, the sentence would attain a monotone (*ekaśruti*) and so forth, lacking the equal accent of truth. Indeed, in the case of the word "dāśivom" ending in the vowel 'o', the particle "om" follows.
The *subrahmaṇya* [ends with] "oṃ," the supreme form; "sava" and so forth are [chanted] everywhere.
In the *Āraṇyaka*, however, at the end of the sentence, "namaḥ" is said to be acute (*udātta*).
Indeed, for those [deities] of great power, the preceding [syllable] is likewise [acute]. Thus it is sung.
And immediately: *sadyo vāmadevāya*, *ṛtaṃ satyameva ca*, *bhūḥ prapadye*, *sarvo vai*, and *namaḥ*—these should be uttered with the *svarita* accent;
for from this arises the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of speech, wherein there is nothing whatsoever [that remains unmanifest].
The conclusion is that all questions concerning Nārāyaṇa have been fully expounded;
